title: Kafka Failures and Retries
summary: Separate publication from processing, add bounded listener retries, and preserve failed records.

sources.title: Engineering Digest: Kafka Fallback: What if Kafka doesn't work ?

richText: Publication failures
KafkaTemplate.send
c
can fail immediately or complete its future exceptionally later.
A
try/catch
c
around
send
c
alone misses the later failure.
Waiting for the future or attaching a completion callback exposes the publication result.
A wait timeout means the caller stopped waiting.
Sending email directly after a publish timeout is unsafe as a fallback.
The record may still reach Kafka and trigger another email.
Durable pending publication
An outbox is a database record for an event awaiting publication.
It contains a stable event ID and the payload needed to publish later.
Saving the business change and outbox row in the same database transaction keeps their commit together.
This depends on the database’s transaction support.
A worker publishes pending rows and marks them published after broker acknowledgment.
The schedule can use the method-registration pattern already covered.
A crash after publication and before that update can publish the same event again.
The consumer still needs duplicate handling.
A queued response is justified only after durable storage succeeds.
Logging an event does not store pending work.
Container retry and recovery
DefaultErrorHandler
c
handles exceptions raised by a listener.
A backoff controls how long the container waits between retries.
DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer
c
publishes a record that exhausted its allowed attempts to a dead-letter topic.
This preserves failed input for investigation and a controlled replay.
Boot attaches a
CommonErrorHandler
c
bean to its auto-configured listener container factory.
DefaultErrorHandler
c
implements that interface.
A permanent format error needs correction.
Repeating the same invalid input does not fix it.

example.title: Retry twice, then publish a failed record
description: Each tab names a file relative to the project root. Java `17` and Maven are required. `mvn spring-boot:run` starts this example after its external requirements are configured.
The tabs include the producer runner, listener, topic declarations, error handler, broker settings, application class, and complete build file.
A local broker must be reachable through `KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS` and permit topic creation and publication. These settings use an unauthenticated local demonstration broker.
The original topic has one partition.
The dead-letter topic has one matching partition so recovery can use the original partition number.
The broker must permit creation and publication to `weekly-sentiments.DLT`.
This example handles failures after string deserialization, including JSON parsing inside the listener.
Deserializer failures before listener invocation need a separate `ErrorHandlingDeserializer` configuration.
The runner sends a valid event on startup. Changing its `version` to `2` demonstrates immediate dead-letter recovery. Invalid JSON demonstrates the retryable parsing failure.
explanation: The destination name is supplied explicitly.
`FixedBackOff(1000L, 2L)` waits one second between two retries.
A retryable failure gets up to three processing attempts including the initial attempt.
`IllegalArgumentException` skips those retries and goes to recovery.
`DigestListener` in these tabs uses that exception for an invalid event contract.
`setFailIfSendResultIsError(true)` makes failed dead-letter publication fail recovery.
The failed record must not be treated as safely recovered when publication failed.
After successful recovery, the container can progress past the recovered record under its acknowledgment policy.
This is not successful business processing.
A dead-letter topic needs monitoring and an explicit replay process.
It is not an automatic repair.

richText: Repeated delivery and external actions
A stable event ID lets a processor recognize a repeated event.
An in-memory set loses that information on restart.
Producer idempotence prevents some duplicate writes caused by producer retries.
It does not make an email happen once.
Kafka transactions support exactly-once behavior for supported Kafka read-process-write flows.
Ordinary SMTP submission is outside that transaction.
Sending email before recording completion risks a duplicate after a crash.
Recording completion before sending risks a lost email.
Provider-supported idempotent submission can close that gap.
Otherwise the application must choose and document its remaining duplicate or loss behavior.
Retry counts, failed-record counts, and consumer lag need monitoring.
Lag measures how far group consumption is behind available records.
